content:
The homepage of an online store has one job: get each visitor to the right products as quickly as possible, and convince a first-time visitor that the store is real and safe to buy from. When we plan ecommerce website development in Pune for a new client, we start the homepage not with a banner design but with two lists: the three or four routes most shoppers will take into the catalogue, and the questions a stranger needs answered before trusting the store. Everything on the page should serve one of those two lists. This guide walks through what to put on an ecommerce homepage, section by section, how it should behave on a phone, what to leave out, and how to tell whether it is working.

It is written for founders, D2C brand owners and retail businesses moving online. It assumes you are using Shopify, WooCommerce or a custom platform; the principles are the same.

## Why the homepage matters less, and more, than you think

Many shoppers never see your homepage. Someone who clicks a Google Shopping ad or an Instagram product post lands on a product page; someone searching "cotton kurta for women" may land on a collection page. For those visitors, the [product page](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-product-page-conversion-checklist-2026) and the [collection page](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-collection-page-seo-content-2026) do the selling.

But the homepage still carries weight in three ways:

1. **Returning and direct visitors** (people who type your name, tap your bookmark or come from a WhatsApp message) usually arrive there.
2. **Visitors who landed elsewhere and are not yet convinced** often tap the logo to "see what this store is" before buying. The homepage becomes the trust check.
3. **Search engines** treat the homepage as the most important page on the site; its internal links tell them which categories matter most.

So the homepage is less a shop window and more a combined signpost and credibility page.

## Start with routes, not banners

Before any design, write down how people actually choose products in your category. Common routes are:

- **By category or product type**: sarees, kurtas, dupattas; or mattresses, pillows, bedsheets.
- **By need or occasion**: wedding wear, office wear, gifts under ₹1,000, Diwali hampers.
- **By person**: men, women, kids.
- **By collection or launch**: new arrivals, bestsellers, a festive edit.
- **By search**: shoppers who already know what they want, especially in stores with large catalogues.

Pick the two or three that cover most shoppers. If you have sales data, look at which collections get the most visits and orders. If you are new, ask your offline staff how customers describe what they want. Those routes become the homepage's main navigation blocks, and they should also match your main menu. Our guide to [site search and category navigation](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-site-search-category-navigation-2026) covers the menu side in detail.

## The homepage, section by section

The order below works for most small and mid-sized stores. Adjust it, but have a reason for every section you add.

### 1. Announcement bar (optional, one message)

A thin strip above the header for one important, current message: a delivery promise you can keep, a festive sale end date, or "Free delivery above ₹999" if that is your actual policy. One message, not a rotating ticker of five. Remove it when there is nothing important to say.

### 2. Header: logo, search, account, cart, menu

On a phone, the header should show the menu icon, logo, search icon (or a visible search field for large catalogues) and cart with an item count. Keep it compact; a header taking a quarter of the screen leaves little room for products. If search is a primary route for your shoppers, show a search box, not just an icon.

### 3. First screen: what you sell and where to start

The first screen a shopper sees on a phone should answer "what is this store?" and give a clear way in. A strong pattern is:

- A short headline that names the product range and what makes it different ("Handloom cotton sarees, woven in Maharashtra"), not a slogan that could belong to any brand.
- One real photograph of your products in use, cropped well for a portrait phone screen.
- One or two buttons to the main routes ("Shop sarees", "New arrivals").

A rotating carousel of four banners is common but rarely the best choice. Usability research groups such as the Nielsen Norman Group and Baymard Institute have documented for years that shoppers tend to ignore auto-rotating carousels, often only see the first slide, and can find them distracting or hard to control. If you do use one, keep it to two or three slides, stop auto-rotation or make it slow, and give each slide a clear text label and link.

### 4. Category tiles

Directly below the first screen, show your main categories as tiles with a photo and a plain label. On a phone, a two-column grid or a horizontally scrolling row both work; whichever you choose, labels must be readable without zooming and every tile must be large enough to tap. Six to eight tiles is plenty; link to a full "All categories" page for the rest.

### 5. Bestsellers or new arrivals

A row of real products with photo, name, price and rating if you have genuine reviews. Choose which to show based on your business: established stores benefit from bestsellers (social proof), fashion and seasonal stores from new arrivals (reason to return). Show prices including any discount clearly, and avoid "Sold out" products in this row.

### 6. Trust block

This is where a first-time visitor decides whether to risk an order. Keep it factual and specific:

- Delivery: where you deliver, typical timelines you can actually meet, and charges or thresholds.
- Payment options you genuinely support, including cash on delivery if offered.
- Returns or exchange policy in one sentence, linked to the full page.
- Contact: a phone number, WhatsApp, email and, if you have one, a physical address in Pune. A real address is a strong trust signal for Indian shoppers.

Four short items with icons work well. Every claim must be true and match your policy pages; a "7-day easy returns" badge that contradicts your returns page is worse than no badge.

### 7. Social proof

Genuine customer reviews with names (or initials) and the product bought, ratings from your review app, press mentions you can link to, or photos customers have shared with permission. Do not invent reviews or copy them from elsewhere; India's Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 and the BIS standard IS 19000:2022 on online consumer reviews both set expectations about genuine, unbiased review practices, and fake reviews damage trust when they are spotted.

### 8. Story section (short)

Two or three sentences about who you are and why the products are made the way they are, with a link to the full About page. For craft, handmade, organic and regional brands, this is a real selling point; for a general electronics store it may not be needed.

### 9. Shop-by-need or gifting row (optional)

If your shoppers think in occasions (festivals, weddings, birthdays, corporate gifting), a row of occasion collections can outperform category tiles. Rotate it with the season.

### 10. Newsletter or WhatsApp opt-in

A simple sign-up with a clear reason to join ("New arrivals every Friday") and an honest explanation of what you will send. Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, consent must be specific and informed; do not pre-tick boxes or bury the purpose. Avoid a full-screen pop-up on arrival on mobile: Google has warned for years that intrusive interstitials that cover content can harm the experience, and shoppers dislike them. We discuss this in our guide to pop-ups, exit offers and cookie banners.

### 11. Footer

Policies (shipping, returns, privacy, terms), contact details, business name and address, and links to main categories. The footer is where careful shoppers go to check you are legitimate, so keep it complete and current.

## What to leave out

The most common homepage mistakes we fix in redesigns are additions, not omissions:

- **Autoplaying background video** that is heavy on mobile data and delays the first screen.
- **Several large banners stacked one after another**, each saying a variation of "Sale".
- **Instagram feed embeds** that load slowly and pull visitors away to another app. Link to your profile instead, or show a few curated images hosted on your own site.
- **Chat widgets, pop-ups and spin-the-wheel offers all at once**, competing for the same small screen.
- **Rows of products that are mostly out of stock.**
- **Generic stock photography** that does not show your actual products.
- **Long paragraphs of keyword-heavy text** at the bottom of the page written for search engines rather than people. A short, useful introduction to what you sell is fine; stuffing is not, and it can do more harm than good.

## Speed and mobile behaviour

The homepage is often the heaviest page on a store because it carries the most images and scripts. That matters because Google's Core Web Vitals (Largest Contentful Paint, Interaction to Next Paint and Cumulative Layout Shift) are measured on real visitors' devices, and many Indian shoppers use mid-range Android phones on mobile data.

Practical rules:

- Make the first-screen image the right size for phones, served in a modern format such as WebP or AVIF, and do not lazy-load it (lazy-load the images below it instead).
- Reserve space for images and banners so the layout does not jump as they load.
- Limit fonts to one or two families and a few weights.
- Audit apps and plugins that inject scripts on every page: review widgets, chat, analytics, heatmaps, pop-ups. Each should earn its place.
- Test on a real mid-range phone, not only on a desktop with fast Wi-Fi.

Our guide to [store speed and Core Web Vitals](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-store-speed-core-web-vitals-2026) goes through measurement and fixes in detail.

## Accessibility basics on the homepage

- Every image that conveys information (category tiles, banners with text) needs meaningful alt text; purely decorative images should have empty alt text.
- Text on banners must have enough contrast against the background, and important text should be real text, not baked into the image, so it scales and can be read by screen readers and search engines.
- Carousels need visible pause controls and keyboard access.
- Headings should follow a logical order: one H1 that describes the store, then H2s for each section.

These steps help shoppers with disabilities, older shoppers and anyone in bright sunlight on a phone.

## SEO considerations for an ecommerce homepage

- **Title tag and meta description**: say what you sell and, if relevant, where ("Handloom Cotton Sarees Online | [Brand], Pune"). Avoid just the brand name.
- **One clear H1**, usually describing the store's range.
- **Links to main categories in plain HTML**, so search engines can follow them.
- **Organization and WebSite structured data** with your logo, contact details and social profiles.
- **A short, genuinely useful introduction** to your range, not a block of keywords.

The homepage rarely ranks for specific product searches; collection and product pages do that. The homepage's SEO job is to rank for your brand and to pass authority to the categories that matter.

## Different stores, different homepages

| Store type | Lead with | Worth adding | Usually skip |
|---|---|---|---|
| Single-product or small range (e.g. a skincare D2C brand with 8 products) | The hero product and its main benefit | Ingredients or proof, reviews, comparison of the range | Category tiles |
| Fashion or seasonal | New arrivals and current edit | Shop by occasion, size guide link | Long brand story at the top |
| Large catalogue (e.g. home goods, hardware, stationery) | Search and category tiles | Bestsellers by category, brand tiles | Big lifestyle banners |
| Regional or craft brand | Story and product photography | Maker stories, care instructions | Generic discount banners |
| B2B or wholesale | Trade login and catalogue access | Bulk enquiry, minimum order details | Consumer offers |

## How to tell if the homepage works

Set up analytics events and look at these monthly:

- **Click-through from the homepage**: what share of homepage visitors click into a category, product or search? If many leave without clicking anything, the routes are not clear.
- **Which sections get clicks**: Microsoft Clarity or a similar heatmap tool, or GA4 events on section links, show whether shoppers use the tiles, the bestseller row or the search.
- **Search usage from the homepage**: high use may mean the navigation is not matching how people think.
- **Conversion rate of sessions that include the homepage** compared with those that do not.
- **Mobile versus desktop behaviour**, separately.

Change one thing at a time and give each change enough time and traffic to judge. Small stores rarely have enough traffic for formal A/B tests; a before-and-after comparison over comparable weeks is more realistic.

## An illustrative example

Consider a Pune-based home textiles brand whose homepage opens with a four-slide auto-rotating banner, followed by an Instagram feed and a newsletter pop-up. Heatmaps show most mobile visitors scroll past the banner without tapping, and many leave from the homepage. The redesign replaces the carousel with one product photograph and two buttons ("Shop bedsheets", "Shop cushion covers"), adds category tiles and a bestseller row, moves the newsletter sign-up into the page, and replaces the Instagram embed with a link. The team then compares homepage click-through and orders over the following weeks. This is an invented example to show the method, not a description of a real client or a guaranteed result.

## Frequently asked questions

### What should be on an ecommerce homepage?
A clear statement of what you sell, links to the two or three main ways shoppers choose products (categories, occasions or collections), a row of real products, factual trust information about delivery, payment, returns and contact, genuine reviews and a complete footer with policies.

### Are homepage sliders bad for ecommerce?
They are often ineffective. Usability research has found that shoppers frequently ignore auto-rotating carousels and see only the first slide. A single strong image with clear buttons usually works better. If you use a slider, keep it short, slow or manual, and clearly labelled.

### How many products should be on the homepage?
Enough to show what you sell, not your whole catalogue. One or two rows of bestsellers or new arrivals, four to eight products each, is typical. Use category tiles and search to lead shoppers to the rest.

### Does the homepage help ecommerce SEO?
Yes, mainly for searches for your brand and by passing authority to your main categories through clear links. Product and collection pages are what usually rank for specific product searches, so put most SEO effort there.

### Should I use a pop-up on my store homepage?
Avoid full-screen pop-ups as soon as someone arrives on mobile; they block content and annoy shoppers. If you want sign-ups, use an inline section, a small banner, or a delayed and easily dismissed prompt.
